questions.qtext:
A router receives a $1500$-byte IPv4 packet (including a $20$-byte IP header), with IP Identification field set to $\mathbf{x}$, the MF (More Fragments) flag set to $1$, and the DF (Don't Fragment) flag set to $0$. The router needs to forward the packet over a link with an MTU of $1000$ bytes, so fragmentation is required.

Which of the following statements about the IP header fields of the second fragment are correct?

options.text: The value of the Identification field in the second fragment is $\mathbf{x}$
The Total Length field in the second fragment is $\mathbf{5 2 0}$ bytes
The Fragment Offset field in the second fragment is $\mathbf{9 8 0}$
The MF (More Fragments) flag in the second fragment is $\mathbf{1}$

questions.solution:
Answer: A, D

Selected solution (score: 4)

The key observation is the value of the MF (More Fragments) flag.

  • IP Identification = x
  • MF = 1
  • DF = 0

Since MF = 1, the received packet is already a fragment of a larger IP datagram. The router must fragment this packet further because the outgoing MTU is only 1000 bytes.

In IPv4, all fragments of the same original datagram carry the same Identification field.

$$ \text{Identification in second fragment} = x $$

Option A is Correct.

The packet contains 1480 bytes of payload (1500 − 20).

With MTU = 1000 bytes, the first new fragment can carry 976 bytes of payload, leaving:

$$ 1480 - 976 = 504 $$

Therefore, the second fragment size is:

$$ 504 + 20 = 524 \text{ bytes} $$

Hence, Option B is Incorrect (not 520 bytes).

The Fragment Offset is measured in units of 8 bytes.

$$ \frac{976}{8} = 122 $$

Thus, the offset of the second fragment is 122, not 980.

Option C is Incorrect.

Since the original fragment already had MF = 1, there are more fragments of the original datagram after it. Therefore, every fragment created from it must also have:

$$ MF = 1 $$

Option D is Correct.

Source solution 2 (score: 10)

Given:

  • Total packet size = 1500 Bytes
  • IP Header size = 20 Bytes
  • MTU = 1000 Bytes
Therefore, IP Payload size = 1500 - 20 = 1480 Bytes
Also, MTU can have max payload of 1000 - 20 = 980 Bytes.
IP fragment offset must be a multiple of 8 bytes. (980 / 8 = 122.5).
So we choose 976B as the largest valid payload size for each fragment.
Therefore, there will be 2 fragments.
Fragment 1:
  • Payload = 976 Bytes
  • Total length = 976 + 20 = 996 Bytes
  • Fragment offset = 0
  • MF = 1
  • identification = x
Fragment 2
  • Payload = 504 Bytes
  • Total length = 504+20 = 524 Bytes
  • Fragment offset = 976/8 = 122
  • MF = 0 (because it is the last fragment of the current packet)
  • Identification = x
Answer : A only

answers is A,D

questions.qtext: During normal IP packet forwarding by a router, which of the following packet fields are updated?
questions.solution:
Answer: C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Following packet fields are changed:
1. IP header TTL : Each router decrements TTL by 1 to prevent forwarding loops.

2. IP header checksum : The header checksum need to be recalculated since the TTL value changed.

Answer: C, D

questions.qtext:
An IP router uses longest prefix matching and has the following forwarding table:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\\
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Prefix} & \text{Interface} \\
\hline
128.2.0.0/24 & \text{Interface 1} \\
128.2.1.0/24 & \text{Interface 2} \\
128.2.2.0/24 & \text{Interface 2} \\
128.2.3.0/24 & \text{Interface 3} \\
\hline
\end{array} \\
\\
\text{The router can only store $3$ prefix entries.} \\
\text{Which of the following options gives a functionally equivalent forwarding table?} \\
\\
\text{A.} \\
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Prefix} & \text{Interface} \\
\hline
128.2.0.0/24 & \text{Interface 1} \\
128.2.1.0/23 & \text{Interface 2} \\
128.2.3.0/24 & \text{Interface 3} \\
\hline
\end{array} \\
\\
\text{B.} \\
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Prefix} & \text{Interface} \\
\hline
128.2.0.0/24 & \text{Interface 1} \\
128.2.1.0/24 & \text{Interface 2} \\
128.2.2.0/24 & \text{Interface 2} \\
\hline
\end{array} \\
\\
\text{C.} \\
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Prefix} & \text{Interface} \\
\hline
128.2.0.0/22 & \text{Interface 2} \\
128.2.0.0/24 & \text{Interface 1} \\
128.2.3.0/24 & \text{Interface 3} \\
\hline
\end{array} \\
\\
\text{D.} \\
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Prefix} & \text{Interface} \\
\hline
128.2.0.0/22 & \text{Interface 1} \\
128.2.1.0/24 & \text{Interface 2} \\
128.2.3.0/24 & \text{Interface 3} \\
\hline
\end{array}
\end{array}
$$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 3)
$128.2.0.0/22$ covers the range $128.2.0.0 - 128.2.3.255$, so it broadly defaults to Interface 2.

More specific entries like $/24$ for $128.2.0.0$ and $128.2.3.0$ override it using longest prefix match.

Thus, routing behavior remains consistent with the original $4$-entry table.
Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Based on the principles of Longest Prefix Matching, here is the step-by-step solution to find the functionally equivalent forwarding table.

Analysis of the Original Table

The router has four contiguous Class C (/24) subnets:

  1. 128.2.0.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 1

  2. 128.2.1.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 2

  3. 128.2.2.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 2

  4. 128.2.3.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 3

We need to compress this into 3 entries. The standard way to do this is to create a "default" aggregate route that covers all four subnets and points to the most common interface, then add specific entries for the exceptions.

Aggregation Strategy

  1. Identify the Supernet:

    The four subnets 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 can be aggregated into a single /22 block: 128.2.0.0/22. This block covers the range 128.2.0.0 to 128.2.3.255.

  2. Identify the "Majority" Interface:

    Interface 2 is the destination for two of the subnets (1.0 and 2.0). This makes it the best candidate for the aggregate route.

    • Proposed Rule 1: 128.2.0.0/22 $\rightarrow$ Interface 2

  3. Identify Exceptions:

    Now we need to add specific rules for the subnets that should not go to Interface 2.

    • Subnet 0.0 needs to go to Interface 1.

      • Proposed Rule 2: 128.2.0.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 1

    • Subnet 3.0 needs to go to Interface 3.

      • Proposed Rule 3: 128.2.3.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 3

Verification of Option C

Let's test Option C against our requirements using Longest Prefix Match:

  • Packet to 128.2.0.x:

    • Matches 128.2.0.0/22 (Interface 2).

    • Matches 128.2.0.0/24 (Interface 1).

    • Result: Longest match is /24. Goes to Interface 1. (Correct)

  • Packet to 128.2.1.x:

    • Matches 128.2.0.0/22 (Interface 2).

    • Does not match any specific /24 entry.

    • Result: Goes to Interface 2. (Correct)

  • Packet to 128.2.2.x:

    • Matches 128.2.0.0/22 (Interface 2).

    • Does not match any specific /24 entry.

    • Result: Goes to Interface 2. (Correct)

  • Packet to 128.2.3.x:

    • Matches 128.2.0.0/22 (Interface 2).

    • Matches 128.2.3.0/24 (Interface 3).

    • Result: Longest match is /24. Goes to Interface 3. (Correct)

Why other options fail:

  • A: The entry 128.2.1.0/23 is problematic. In CIDR, a /23 block starting at .1 is invalid (it would start at .0). Even if interpreted loosely, this table structure doesn't correctly cover the 2.0 subnet or misdirects others.

  • B: This table is missing an entry for the 128.2.3.0 subnet entirely. Packets for 3.0 would be dropped.

  • D: The aggregate route points to Interface 1. This means 128.2.2.0 (which has no specific entry) would default to Interface 1, which is incorrect (it should go to Interface 2).

Correct Answer

Option C

questions.qtext: Suppose computers $A$ and $B$ have IP addresses $10.105.1.113$ and $10.105.1.91$, respectively, and they both use the same netmask $N$. Which of the values of $N$ given below should not be used if $A$ and $B$ should belong to the same network?
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Goal: For each netmask, find the one that results in different network addresses for A and B.

In the given options, we observe that the Netmasks only differ in the 4th octet; so we only need to expand the 4th octet to binary format and check which one results in different network addresses for A and B.

For computer A : 10.105.1.(0111 0001)

For computer B: 10.105.1.(01011011)

While checking you will notice that for option D:

255.255.255.(1110 0000) is the netmask.

The third bit from the left in the 4th octet is different for A and B. Thus option D will result in different network addresses for A and B.

Answer: D

questions.qtext:
An IP datagram is fragmented into three packets.

The following table shows the first 20 bytes of each IP fragment, starting from the IP header (hex values):

📦 Packet #1📦 Packet #2📦 Packet #3
\(\texttt{45 00 02 54}\)\(\texttt{45 00 01 5a}\)\(\texttt{45 00 02 54}\)
\(\texttt{42 d8 20 48}\)\(\texttt{42 d8 00 90}\)\(\texttt{42 d8 20 00}\)
\(\texttt{40 11 fe af}\)\(\texttt{40 11 1f 62}\)\(\texttt{40 11 fe f7}\)
\(\texttt{0a 00 01 02}\)\(\texttt{0a 00 01 02}\)\(\texttt{0a 00 01 02}\)
\(\texttt{0a 00 01 c8}\)\(\texttt{0a 00 01 c8}\)\(\texttt{0a 00 01 c8}\)

Based on this information, what is the correct order of the fragments for reassembling the original IP datagram?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

In an IPv4 fragment, the second row (i.e., bytes 7 and 8 of the IP header) contains a 16-bit field:

Flags + Fragment Offset (13 bits offset, 3 bits flags)

This field is provided as two hexadecimal bytes.

PacketFlags + OffsetLast 13 Bits (Hex)
Packet #120 48048
Packet #200 90090
Packet #320 00000


🔷 Packet #1: 20 48

  • Take last 13 bits → hex = 048
  • Decimal = 72, so offset = \(72 \times 8 = \boxed{576 \text{ bytes}}\)

🔷 Packet #2: 00 90

  • Last 13 bits = 090
  • Decimal = 144, so offset = \(144 \times 8 = \boxed{1152 \text{ bytes}}\)

🔷 Packet #3: 20 00

  • Last 13 bits = 000
  • Decimal = 0, so offset = \(0 \times 8 = \boxed{0 \text{ bytes}}\)

Hence, the correct reassembly sequence is:

\[ \boxed{\text{Packet #3} \rightarrow \text{Packet #1} \rightarrow \text{Packet #2}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \textbf{Option B} \]

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Task: Determine the correct order of fragments to reassemble the original IP datagram.

Analysis:

  1. Identify Fragments: We have Packet #1, #2, and #3. We need to look at the Offset and MF (More Fragments) flag in the IP header.

    • Offset: The 13-bit Fragment Offset is in the 2nd row, last 2 bytes (combined with Flags).

    • Hex Data (Row 2): 42 d8 ...

    • 4 = 0100 (Flags + Offset bits). First 3 bits are flags.

      • Bit 0: Reserved (0).

      • Bit 1: DF (1).

      • Bit 2: MF (0).

    • Wait, let's look closer at the values provided.

      • Packet #1: Row 2 is 42 d8. 4 is 0100. Flag is 010 (DF=1, MF=0). Offset is 0 1101 1000? No, let's re-examine the standard header layout.

      • Byte 0: Version/IHL (45).

      • Byte 6-7: Flags/Offset.

      • Packet #1: 20 48. 2=0010. Flags=001 (MF=1). Offset=0 0100 1000 (72×8=576).

      • Packet #2: 00 90. 0=0000. Flags=000 (MF=0). Offset=0 1001 0000 (144×8=1152).

      • Packet #3: 20 00. 2=0010. Flags=001 (MF=1). Offset=0.

  2. Ordering:

    • First Fragment: Must have Offset = 0. Packet #3 fits this (Offset = 0).

    • Middle Fragment: Must have Offset > 0 and MF = 1. Packet #1 fits this (Offset = 576, MF=1).

    • Last Fragment: Must have Offset > 0 and MF = 0. Packet #2 fits this (Offset = 1152, MF=0).

  3. Sequence: Packet #3 → Packet #1 → Packet #2.

Answer: B. Packet #3 → Packet #1 → Packet #

questions.qtext:
Consider the following IP header. The checksum field is currently set to 0000. The header is being prepared for transmission.

Version
4		IHL
5		Type of Service
00		Total Length
001C
Identification
0001		Flags
0		Fragment Offset
0000
Time to Live
01		Protocol
11		Header Checksum
0000
Source Address
0A0C0E05
Destination Address
0C060709


What value should be written into the checksum field?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

The header is grouped into 2‑byte words (16 bits each).

\[ \begin{array}{r@{\;}l} \texttt{0x 45 00} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 00 1C} &= \texttt{0x 45 1C} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 00 01} &= \texttt{0x 45 1D} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 00 00} &= \texttt{0x 45 1D} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 04 11} &= \texttt{0x 49 2E} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 00 00} &= \texttt{0x 49 2E} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 0A 0C} &= \texttt{0x 53 3A} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 0E 05} &= \texttt{0x 61 3F} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 0C 06} &= \texttt{0x 6D 45} \\ +\ \texttt{0x 07 09} &= \texttt{0x 74 4E} \\ \end{array} \]

\(\text{Final sum} = \texttt{0x 744E}\)

\(\text{1's Complement of } \texttt{0x 744E} = \texttt{0x 8BB1}\)

Source solution 3 (score: 3)

IPv4 Header Checksum Calculation

The correct option is most likely B. 8BB1, assuming a small typo in the question's values (specifically the TTL). Here is the step-by-step calculation based on the image provided.

The Algorithm:

To calculate the IPv4 header checksum:

  1. Divide the header into 16-bit words.

  2. Set the checksum field to 0000.

  3. Sum all the 16-bit words using one's complement arithmetic.

  4. Take the one's complement (invert the bits) of the final sum.

Step 1: Extract 16-bit Words (Hexadecimal)

Based on the image:

  • Word 1: 4500 (Version=4, IHL=5, ToS=00)

  • Word 2: 001C (Total Length = 28 bytes)

  • Word 3: 0001 (Identification)

  • Word 4: 0000 (Flags=0, Fragment Offset=0)

  • Word 5: 0111 (TTL=01, Protocol=11 hex)

  • Word 6: 0000 (Checksum placeholder)

  • Word 7: 0A0C (Source IP: 0A, 0C)

  • Word 8: 0E05 (Source IP: 0E, 05)

  • Word 9: 0C06 (Dest IP: 0C, 06)

  • Word 10: 0709 (Dest IP: 07, 09)

Step 2: Calculate the Sum

We add these hexadecimal values together.

$$\begin{array}{r@{\quad}l} & 4500 \\ + & 001C \\ + & 0001 \\ + & 0000 \\ + & 0111 \\ + & 0A0C \\ + & 0E05 \\ + & 0C06 \\ + & 0709 \\ \hline \textbf{Sum} & \mathbf{714E} \end{array}$$

(Note: The sum 0x714E is less than 0xFFFF, so no carry wrap-around is needed.)

Step 3: Calculate the Checksum

The checksum is the one's complement of the sum 714E.

$$FFFF - 714E = \mathbf{8EB1}$$

Step 4: Analyzing the Options

  • Calculated Checksum: 8EB1

  • Option B: 8BB1

There is a discrepancy of 0x0300 between the calculated value and Option B (8EB1 - 8BB1 = 300). This corresponds exactly to a difference of 3 in the Time to Live (TTL) field (the high byte of Word 5).

  • If the TTL were 4 (instead of 1), Word 5 would be 0411.

  • The Sum would increase by 0300 to become 744E.

  • The Checksum would be FFFF - 744E = 8BB1.

Given that 8BB1 is the only plausible option derived from the data structure, it is highly likely that the intended TTL value in the question was 4.

Answer: B. 8BB1
